screens.body:
A process is a program that's running — its code plus its own private memory plus its current state. Open Spotify and a text editor? That's (at least) two processes.

Each process is isolated: one crashing doesn't corrupt another's memory. That isolation is the OS protecting you.

options: A running program with its own private memory
check.question: A process is…

screens.heading: What is a process?
screens.keyPoint: A process is a running program, isolated from others.

screens.body:
A thread is a single line of execution inside a process — one thing-after-another sequence of instructions. A process starts with one thread, but can spawn more.

Think of a process as a kitchen and threads as cooks. One kitchen, many cooks, all sharing the same ingredients (memory).
screens.heading: What is a thread?
screens.keyPoint: Threads are execution lines sharing one process's memory.

screens.body:
Processes are heavy and isolated — great for safety, expensive to create. Threads are light and share memory — great for speed, risky if they step on each other.

Your browser uses both: separate processes per tab (so one tab's crash doesn't kill the rest), threads inside each tab for speed.

options: One tab's crash can't kill the others
check.question: Why separate processes per browser tab?

screens.heading: Processes vs threads
screens.keyPoint: Processes for safety, threads for speed.

screens.body:
You have maybe 8 CPU cores but 300 processes. The OS fakes simultaneity by context switching: run process A for a few milliseconds, save its state, load process B, repeat.

Each switch costs a little time (saving/loading state), but it's so fast you perceive everything running at once.

options: Saves one process's state and loads another's, very fast
check.question: Context switching…

screens.heading: Context switching

screens.body:
The scheduler is the OS's bouncer — it picks which ready process gets the CPU next. The classic fair policy is round-robin: everyone gets a short time slice, then back of the line.

Priorities can bend the rules: your music player might outrank a background backup so your audio never stutters.

options: Gives every process a fair time slice in turn
check.question: Round-robin scheduling…

screens.heading: Scheduling: who runs next?

screens.body:
Processes move through states: new (being created) → ready (waiting for CPU) → running (on the CPU) → waiting (stuck on something, like disk) → terminated (done).

A process spends most of its life bouncing between ready, running, and waiting. The scheduler manages the whole dance.

check.question: A process stuck on disk I/O is in state…

screens.heading: The life of a process

screens.body:
Node.js runs your backend on a single thread with an event loop — one long line of execution. If your code blocks that thread (a giant loop, a slow sync read), every request waits.

That's why Node has async I/O: instead of blocking, it parks the waiting work and keeps serving others. Same idea as process states, one level up.
screens.heading: Why this matters for you
screens.keyPoint: One blocked thread stalls the whole server.
